title: Claiborne Williams band, Petit's sidemen and visiting bands
summary: The in-demand Williams band, Petit's players Edmond Hall and George Washington, other New Orleans jazzmen working across the lake, and bands advertising dances in town.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: Let me see now. Who else did you mention that you heard over there in those days?

Well, in those days, I'll tell you, one of the most sought-after bands in that part of the country was the Claven Williams Band, from Donisonville. I wish I could tell you more about it, but I can't, other than that it was very much in demand. And as I recall it, they had a rather large band. I think they used eight or ten pieces.
Would they be of the school of Pierron or more like Buddy Petit?
No, I would say more of the school of Pierron or possibly the old tuxedo bands of Celestan and Wrigley.
If you can give me the date on that, that would be good too.
Well, it was in the early 20s, that's about all I close to that.
Early 20s? And who were the people?

Well, the only musicians I recall with Buddy Petit at the time was Edmund Hall on clarinet and a George Washington on trombone. I think there have been several George Washington trombones. I can't tell you which one this was, but there was a George Washington on trombone. Short film? My memory's not good enough. I don't remember. Around the same time, I just mentioned two or three bands there, but there were bands such as, I believe, Silverleaf Band, the Tuxedo Band. And I'm quite sure that Punch Miller and Kid Ory and George Lewis and Bichet and all of those jazzmen played over there at some time or other, because it was quite a place for them to get work, and I think they enjoyed getting over there on weekends too. And I might mention this, might be of some interest, that if there were to be a dance, for instance, on a Saturday night, when the band got into town, and most of those small towns are usually a main street and a drugstore, and they would get either in front of the drugstore or maybe in front of the one theatre in the town and play for a half hour or so, publicizing the dance that night. In New Orleans here, as you know, they used to go around in the wagons to publicize the dances and prize fights and whatnot.
